description: For twelve and a half years Mahāvīra meditated in silence, naked after thirteen months, in empty houses, cremation grounds and under trees; in Lāḍha he was beaten and dogs were set on him; he took no medicine and fasted long, bearing all without anger.
Under a śāla tree by the Ṛjupālikā, squatting in the sun after a waterless fast, in pure meditation, the infinite and complete knowledge and perception (kevala) arose in him.

Indrabhūti Gautama, sent away by Mahāvīra on his last night, learned of the nirvāṇa, grieved, reflected that the Jina had been without attachment, cut his own bond of affection and attained omniscience before dawn (tradition's account).

At the conception of a Tīrthaṅkara his mother sees fourteen great dreams (sixteen in Digambara accounts) — elephant, bull, lion, the goddess Śrī and the rest — which the dream-interpreters explain as signs of a son who will be a world-emperor or a Jina.

Bāhubali stood a year in body-abandonment until creepers climbed his limbs and ants built hills at his feet; omniscience came only when his last inner obstacle fell (pride, in the Śvetāmbara account; the thought of his brother's land, in the Digambara account).

Ṛṣabha's mother Marudevī, weeping for her son, saw from elephant-back the splendour of his assembly, understood detachment, and attained omniscience and liberation at once — the first of this era (Śvetāmbara account).

Sthūlabhadra, having learned the Pūrvas, took the form of a lion to show his power to his visiting sisters; Bhadrabāhu judged him unfit and withheld the meaning of the last four Pūrvas — the tradition's warning that displaying powers costs the teaching.

The fiery power (tejoleśyā) Gośāla gained by austerity, used to burn two of Mahāvīra's monks; directed at Mahāvīra it turned back and consumed Gośāla — told as a warning against powers used with passion.

As Pārśva meditated, the god Meghamālin (his old enemy Kamaṭha) sent storm and flood; the serpent-king Dharaṇendra and Padmāvatī, whom Pārśva had once saved from fire, sheltered him with their hoods — the scene of his images.
The omniscient's teaching issues as a single divine sound, without movement of the lips, understood by gods, humans and animals each in their own speech.
The gods raise a circular assembly of concentric walls and gateways in which beings of every kind sit in twelve assemblies, animals without enmity, while the Jina appears to face all four directions.
With burning coals heaped on his head, Gajasukumāla regarded his tormentor as a helper in shedding karma, kept pure meditation and attained liberation that night.
Reminded by Mahāvīra, Megha recalled his former birth as an elephant (jātismaraṇa) and was restored to steadiness in his vows.
The layman Ānanda gained clairvoyance (avadhi-jñāna) of great range through his vows and stages; Gautama doubted that a layman could see so far and was told by Mahāvīra to ask his forgiveness.
The body of the ascetic Dhanya, worn by fasting, is described limb by limb as dry and shrunken, praised by Mahāvīra (restricted theme: recorded as the text's description only).
Kundakunda is said to have gone by supernatural power to the living Tīrthaṅkara Sīmandhara in Videha and to have heard the teaching directly (Digambara legend).

The nun Mṛgāvatī, rebuked by Candanā for returning late, repented so deeply that she attained omniscience; Candanā, asking her pupil's forgiveness, attained it too (Śvetāmbara story; low confidence on the source).
